summary: This informational memo describes the Data Link Switching Remote Access Protocol, used between workstations and routers to carry SNA and NetBIOS traffic over TCP connections. It was replaced by RFC 2114.

eli5.summary: Old office systems spoke their own language; this protocol packs their messages inside ordinary Internet envelopes so they can travel.

questions: data link switching remote access protocol
subtitle: A protocol for carrying legacy network traffic over TCP connections.

tldr.problem: Data Link Switching (DLSw) was designed for router-to-router connections to carry SNA and NetBIOS traffic, but when implemented on individual workstations, the number of TCP sessions to the central router grew uncontrollably.
tldr.mechanism: RFC 2106 introduces the Data Link Switching Remote Access Protocol (DRAP), which replaces the direct peer-to-peer model with a client/server architecture. Workstations (clients) connect to a single router (server) via a single TCP connection, and the server acts as a proxy to the rest of the DLSw network.
tldr.outcome: DRAP solved the scalability problem by dramatically reducing the number of TCP sessions needed, making it practical to deploy DLSw on large numbers of workstations. It was replaced by RFC 2114, which provided enhancements to the protocol.

today: RFC 2106 is an Informational RFC and has been obsoleted by RFC 2114, which refined the DRAP protocol based on implementation experience. DRAP has largely been superseded by more modern approaches to virtualizing legacy networks, but the protocol remains documented for systems that use it.

sections.title: The Scalability Problem
sections.content:
DLSw (Data Link Switching), defined in RFC 1795, was designed to carry Systems Network Architecture (SNA) and NetBIOS traffic over TCP/IP networks. It worked well between routers because there were relatively few of them.

But when software vendors began implementing DLSw on workstations, the problem became clear: each workstation needed a separate DLSw session to the central router, and if a network added hundreds or thousands of workstations, the router would have to maintain hundreds or thousands of peer connections. This did not scale.

DRAP addresses this by introducing a client/server model instead of peer-to-peer. A workstation connects to the router as a client; the router is the server. All workstations share a single server connection to the rest of the network, dramatically reducing the load on the router.
sections.eli5: Imagine a post office where each person in town has their own direct line to the central post office. DRAP is like hiring postal workers to act as intermediaries instead.

sections.title: Client/Server Architecture and MAC Addressing
sections.content:
DRAP introduces a three-layer architecture: workstations (DLSw clients), regional routers (DLSw/DRAP servers), and a central router (the hub of the DLSw network). A workstation sends a CAN_U_REACH frame to its server asking 'can you reach this station?' The server responds with I_CAN_REACH or I_CANNOT_REACH. Once a reachable station is found, the workstation sends a START_DL frame to establish a link.

A key innovation is dynamic MAC address resolution. When a workstation connects via PPP (Point-to-Point Protocol) to a router, it has only an IP address, not a MAC address. DRAP lets the server dynamically assign a MAC address to the client during the CAP_XCHANGE (capability exchange) phase. The client either provides its own MAC address or requests one from the server. This eliminates the need for manual configuration of MAC addresses on every workstation.
sections.eli5: Rather than assigning a street address to every person before they can mail a letter, the post office assigns temporary addresses as needed when people arrive.

sections.title: The DRAP Protocol and Frame Types
sections.content:
DRAP uses a simple 4-byte header for all frames: Protocol ID (4 bits set to 1000), Version (4 bits set to 0001), Message Type (1 byte), and Packet Length (2 bytes). The message type field identifies what kind of message the frame carries.

The RFC defines 20 message types covering discovery (CAN_U_REACH, I_CAN_REACH, I_CANNOT_REACH), circuit setup (START_DL, DL_STARTED, START_DL_FAILED), data transfer (DATA_FRAME, INFO_FRAME, XID_FRAME), circuit teardown (HALT_DL, DL_HALTED), flow control (FCM_FRAME), and peer management (CAP_XCHANGE, CLOSE_PEER_REQUEST, PEER_TEST_REQ). Each frame type carries context-specific data after the header, followed by optional user data (the actual SNA or NetBIOS payload).
sections.eli5: Every message has a label saying what it is (discovery, setup, data, or goodbye), and the post office (server) knows how to handle each label.

sections.title: Data Formats and Connection Setup
sections.content:
The START_DL frame establishes a virtual circuit between two stations. It carries the host and client MAC addresses, the source and destination Service Access Points (SAPs), and a session ID created by the initiating station. The target responds with a DL_STARTED frame that includes its own session ID, completing the handshake.

The Largest Frame Size field uses the IEEE 802.1D standard format to negotiate the maximum frame size the client can accept. The Initial Window Size field, borrowed from DLSw, sets the flow control window. For XID (Exchange Identification) frames and data frames, DRAP carries the payload in a generic structure with a destination session ID, flow control flags, and the user data itself.

Connection teardown uses HALT_DL (with acknowledgment expected) or HALT_DL_NOACK (without). The server can also suspend a TCP session using a CLOSE_PEER_REQUEST with a reason code (shutdown, suspend, or no MAC address available), and the client responds with CLOSE_PEER_RESPONSE.
sections.eli5: Setting up a connection is like opening an account at the post office: you agree on what size letters you can handle, and you get a session number to track your mail.

sections.title: Capability Exchange and Optional Extensions
sections.content:
The CAP_XCHANGE frame lets the client and server exchange capabilities. The client can signal that it supports NetBIOS traffic, TCP listen mode (staying registered even after the TCP session drops), and other features via a 1-byte flags field. The server checks if the MAC address is unique and either accepts it or assigns a new one.

Beyond the basic capability flags, implementors can optionally send Control Vectors: variable-length structures with a type field. Two types are defined: SAP_LIST (which SAPs the client supports) and VENDOR_CODE (vendor identification). The RFC encourages implementations to ignore unknown Control Vectors for future compatibility.

For peer-level keepalive, DRAP defines PEER_TEST_REQ and PEER_TEST_RSP frames. If the sender does not receive a response within a recommended 60 seconds, and this happens three times in a row, the sender closes the TCP session and terminates all circuits on it.
sections.eli5: The client tells the server 'I speak NetBIOS and I can remember you even if I hang up the phone' and the server confirms with a MAC address the client will use for all future mail.

fields.name: Protocol ID / Version
fields.desc: First 4 bits: Protocol ID (1000), last 4 bits: Version (0001).

fields.name: Packet Length
fields.desc: Total length of header, DRAP data, and user data in bytes.
